content: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS) is a type of epilepsy that typically begins before the age of eight. It is characterized by multiple types of seizures, a specific pattern on an electroencephalogram (EEG), and resistance to medications. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and tolerability of anti-seizure medications (ASMs) for treating LGS. The review included 11 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1,277 participants, with follow-up periods ranging from approximately 11 to 112 weeks. All studies investigated ASMs as add-on therapies rather than monotherapy. Below are the findings for specific ASMs: 1. Cannabidiol (CBD): Two studies compared add-on cannabidiol with placebo in children, adolescents, and adults. High-certainty evidence showed that 82 more people per 1,000 experienced adverse events (AEs) leading to study discontinuation with cannabidiol compared to placebo (risk ratio [RR] 6.62, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.56 to 28.15). Insufficient data were available to calculate the proportion of participants achieving seizure reduction. 2. Cinromide: One study evaluated add-on cinromide in children and adolescents. Very low-certainty evidence suggested that 35 more people per 1,000 achieved a 50% or greater reduction in seizures compared to placebo (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.47 to 2.86). The study did not report AEs leading to study discontinuation. 3. Clobazam: One study compared add-on clobazam (three doses) with placebo. High-certainty evidence indicated that 106 more people per 1,000 experienced AEs leading to study discontinuation with clobazam compared to placebo (RR 4.12, 95% CI 1.01 to 16.87). The study did not report overall seizure cessation or reduction. 4. Felbamate: One study assessed add-on felbamate in 73 participants. No cases of seizure cessation were observed during the treatment phase. Low-certainty evidence suggested that 53 more people per 1,000 were seizure-free during an EEG recording at the end of treatment compared to placebo (RR 2.92, 95% CI 0.32 to 26.77). Low-certainty evidence showed that one fewer person per 1,000 experienced AEs leading to study discontinuation compared to placebo (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.06 to 14.97). 5. Lamotrigine: Two studies evaluated add-on lamotrigine. High-certainty evidence showed that 176 more people per 1,000 achieved a 50% or greater reduction in seizures compared to placebo (RR 2.12, 95% CI 1.19 to 3.76). Low-certainty evidence suggested that 40 fewer people per 1,000 experienced AEs leading to study discontinuation compared to placebo (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.13 to 1.82). 6. Rufinamide: Two studies investigated add-on rufinamide. High-certainty evidence indicated that 202 more people per 1,000 achieved a 50% or greater reduction in seizures compared to placebo (RR 2.84, 95% CI 1.31 to 6.18). Low-certainty evidence suggested that 105 more people per 1,000 experienced AEs leading to study discontinuation compared to placebo (RR 4.14, 95% CI 0.49 to 34.86). In a separate study comparing rufinamide with another ASM, low-certainty evidence showed three fewer people per 1,000 experienced AEs leading to study discontinuation (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.10 to 9.57). 7. Topiramate: One study evaluated add-on topiramate. Low-certainty evidence suggested a potential for a 75% or greater reduction in seizures (Peto odds ratio 8.22, 99% CI 0.60 to 112.62). No participants experienced AEs leading to study discontinuation. The authors concluded that there is a lack of RCTs investigating monotherapy or head-to-head comparisons of add-on ASMs for LGS. High-certainty evidence supports the use of add-on lamotrigine and rufinamide for reducing seizures, with low-certainty evidence for AEs leading to study discontinuation. Evidence for other ASMs, including cannabidiol, cinromide, clobazam, felbamate, and topiramate, was of low to very low certainty. Future research should focus on overall seizure reduction using automated seizure detection devices, as well as the impact of ASMs on development, cognition, and behavior. Additionally, studies should explore age-specific efficacy and target the underlying causes of LGS.
